https://www.thetimes.com/article/ed-mill.title: Ed Miliband: ‘My relationship with David is not precisely what it was’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/ed-mill.text:
No 10 used to have a nickname for Ed Miliband. It was the early 2000s and he was a political aide in his early thirties working at the Treasury. “I was the go-between between the two sides — Gordon Brown’s office and Tony Blair’s office,” he says. “But Blair’s office had a rude name for me.” Go on, I urge him. “Well, Gordon used to swear a lot,” Miliband says, already laughing. “So Tony’s team called me the ‘emissary from the Planet F***’.”
I am speaking to him in the corner of the library at Stoke Newington secondary school in northeast London and a group of 12-year-olds are mercifully out of earshot. Miliband is in full flow. “The only thing that can drive you through the bullshit is having a project for the country,” he says. “That’s what makes politics worthwhile. You’ve got to believe in something.”
For Miliband, that cause is the small matter of tackling climate change and turning the UK economy green. At 54 he is back on the political front line as Keir Starmer’s shadow secretary of state for energy security and net zero, and — if the polls are to be believed — is on the verge of re-entering government after a gap of 14 years.
He has persuaded Starmer to make transforming Britain into a “clean energy superpower” one of his five “missions” for government. But the price tag — £28 billion a year — has proved controversial, a political stick for the Tories to beat Labour with. Speculation as to whether the pledge will survive until the election is rife.
Miliband is unfazed by the conjecture. “We are going to be sensible and prudent with people’s money,” he says. “As Rachel [Reeves, the shadow chancellor] says, good chancellors and shadow chancellors know when to say no and when to say yes.”
Miliband’s hair is greyer and he has filled out a little, but it is his ease with himself that makes him barely recognisable from the uptight, gawky politician most people will remember from his time as Labour leader from 2010 to 2015. That period started with his unexpected victory over his older brother, David, for the Labour leadership, and ended with what at the time was the party’s worst electoral defeat since 1987, to David Cameron’s Conservatives.
It also included the photograph of him failing to eat a bacon sandwich and the much-mocked “Ed Stone” — a two-tonne slab of limestone on which his pledges for office were carved.
“Being leader of the opposition is like treading on eggshells,” he says. “Every word you say is jumped on, the press is outside your house, 60 million people are commentating on whether you’re doing a good job or not I probably was too strangulated and constrained about what I said. Maybe I was too cautious.”
He admits it took him some time to get over such a humiliating defeat. But his relationship with David, 58, is healing. “It was incredibly hard, that will be obvious,” he says. “Our relationship is not precisely what it was before the 2010 Labour leadership election, but it is an incredibly close relationship and we love each other very much.
He insists he does not regret standing as leader. “I had something to say and we needed a new set of ideas for the Labour Party and where it was going. I deeply regret losing in 2015, but I don’t regret running for leader.”
There are plenty of people in the Labour Party — particularly Blairites — who are still angry over Miliband’s victory over his brother. Peter Mandelson didn’t hold back in a scathing recent analysis on the Times podcast How to win an election: “He woke up one day and it suddenly dawned on him that he knew why New Labour had been so unsuccessful, why it had failed to win all these elections with these huge majorities It occurred to him that he had a much better idea of how to win elections than anyone who had preceded him.”
Miliband dismisses this as an argument of the past. “When a party loses power there are always elements of continuity and elements of change. It strikes me how irrelevant all those labels are now — Blairites, Brownites. I’m not anyone’s ‘-ite’. Keir isn’t anyone’s ‘-ite’.”
Would he run again? Before the words are even out of my mouth he is laughing. “Definitely not — that is cast iron and categorical. Do you know the Sherman oath?” he asks, referring to the American Civil War general William Sherman, who pledged never to stand for office. “If nominated, I will not run. If elected, I will not serve.”
Two weeks before our meeting in Stoke Newington we are 3,400 miles away, in Dubai. It is 30C outside and Miliband is leaning against an air-conditioning unit. He has been playing the role of diplomat, rushing from meeting to meeting, introducing Starmer to world leaders at the Cop28 climate summit. Wearing an open-necked blue shirt and navy trousers, he is savouring the chilled air and looks as though he would climb into the air-con machine if he could.
Miliband is a veteran of United Nations climate talks, having attended his first Cop at Poznan in Poland in 2008 and battled through the night with Gordon Brown and Barack Obama to try to save the Copenhagen climate accord in 2009. So far today he has introduced Starmer to John Kerry, the US climate envoy, and hosted meetings with Xie Zhenhua, the Chinese envoy, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, António Guterres, the UN secretary-general, and Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados. Isn’t all this foreign glad-handing a distraction at a time when Labour should be focusing on domestic issues?
“Some people say this is just a lot of people flying around the world,” he says. “And I understand their scepticism. It is the most imperfect, flawed process. Every country has its own compelling domestic constraints, so we are playing 200-dimensional chess in terms of what happens to our planet and our world. This is a global problem and this is the best process we’ve got.”
Miliband, a self-confessed geek, produces a report from his bag — the UN Emissions Gap report — and declares: “This is my favourite climate document.” Things then get even more exciting: he flips through the pages. “And this is my favourite climate table. It shows us where we are on current policies, in terms of gigatonnes of emissions. Where do we need to be to get below two degrees? Where do we need to be to get below 1.5C? It shows very clearly what we need to do.”
All politicians have a hard time from the press, but Miliband suffered a particularly bruising treatment as Labour leader. His tabloid nickname of “Red Ed” has stuck and is still regularly wheeled out. His marital status was held as a mark against him; when he became Labour leader he had not yet wed his partner, the lawyer Justine Thornton — now, at 53, a High Court judge. His father, the Marxist sociologist Ralph Miliband, who died in 1994 aged 70 when Ed was 24, was denounced by one newspaper as “the man who hated Britain” over a teenage diary entry in which he criticised English patriotism.
“It does teach you resilience,” Miliband says. “But my family has kept me going.”
His parents came to Britain as Jewish refugees. Ralph fled Belgium during the Second World War, and Marion, who is 89, arrived shortly afterwards, having survived the Holocaust in Poland only because she was sheltered by Catholic nuns.
Ed and David grew up in Primrose Hill, north London, but spent stints in Leeds and Boston, Massachusetts, where their father held posts. The brothers attended Haverstock comprehensive and went on to Corpus Christi College, Oxford, where they both studied philosophy, politics and economics, but five years apart.
After university Ed worked for Harriet Harman — then shadow employment minister — from 1994, before joining Brown the following year in the shadow Treasury team. Apart from spells at the London School of Economics and Harvard, he worked in Brown’s office for a decade. In 2002 he met Justine and in 2005 he was elected MP for Doncaster North. When Brown became prime minister in 2007 he immediately joined his cabinet, first as Cabinet Office minister and then as energy and climate change secretary.
He stayed on as an MP after his 2015 defeat but embraced other avenues, writing a book, Go Big: 20 Bold Solutions to Fix Our World, and starting the Reasons to Be Cheerful podcast with the radio presenter Geoff Lloyd. In 2017 he appeared on the Channel 4 talk show The Last Leg dressed as every member of the Norwegian band A-ha while lip-syncing their hit Take on Me.
He also spent far more time with his sons, Daniel, 14, and Samuel, 13. “ I have a transformatively different relationship with my children now than I did when I was leader,” he says.
So why, having got his life back, did he decide to re-enter the political fray? He admits it was initially a dilemma as to whether he should return, but Starmer wooed him over a number of months as he prepared for his own leadership bid in 2020. When Starmer was announced as Labour leader in April that year, he was named in his first shadow cabinet. If Labour wins power later this year Miliband will be one of only a handful of ministers with experience of government — Yvette Cooper and Hilary Benn are the only other shadow cabinet members who served in Brown’s cabinet.
Despite speculation over the cost of Miliband’s green plan, Labour appears to be relying on it as a core part of its offer. “It’s their answer on energy security, it’s their answer on growth, it’s their answer on levelling up,” says the former Labour staffer Joss Garman, now executive director of the European Climate Foundation. “It’s all about green investment: it’s central to all their arguments.”
Back in Stoke Newington we’ve climbed onto the school’s roof to inspect some solar panels. The sky is slate grey. Miliband is in the same navy trousers, now with matching jacket and a padded coat. The heat of Dubai seems very distant.
Yet Miliband is upbeat. Volunteers from Stokey Energy, a community-owned energy company, explain that within the next six months the savings from these solar panels, which were only put in two years ago, will have paid back the cost of installation. “Who would have thought there was enough sunshine here in Hackney to make such a difference,” Miliband says, beaming.
He views this as a proof of concept for one of the ideas central to his “green prosperity plan”. Miliband has drawn up blueprints for a new publicly owned company called GB Energy to help decarbonise the UK power sector completely by 2030, a highly ambitious — and some say unrealistic — target. It will, he says, cut £93 billion from household and business energy bills by the end of the decade.
“We could be doing thousands of projects like this across the country with proper funding,” he says. “It makes total economic sense, because if we invest this money we can produce real savings.”
After the mess of HS2, though, do we really need another bloated public sector project? Rather than HS2, he prefers to compare his vision to the vaccine taskforce, which provided millions of Covid jabs during the height of the pandemic. “The vast majority of this is going to come from private investment. GB Energy won’t be a substitute for the private sector, it’s a partner for the private sector: a partner on the leading edge of new technologies, such as floating wind, where the government can play a role in de-risking.”
He adds: “When the vaccine taskforce was confronted by hurdles, it just had to find ways around them, and this is what this will do.”
His plan isn’t just about energy: there will be a huge scheme to insulate homes, with £6 billion of funding each year by the end of the first parliament; a one-off £8 billion investment to set up a sovereign wealth fund for green industrial infrastructure; £3 billion over a decade to decarbonise the steel industry; £1.8 billion over five years to rebuild Britain’s ports so they are “renewable ready”; £2 billion for gigafactories to put batteries in electric cars; £500 million for green hydrogen.
Miliband also plans to recruit for his mission from outside the Labour Party, including Conservatives: “people like” Alok Sharma, the president of Cop26, and the former energy minister Chris Skidmore, who quit as a Tory MP this month over Rishi Sunak’s plan to expand oil and gas exploration in the North Sea. Miliband has warm words for Theresa May, who passed net zero into law in 2019. “She has a really important, powerful climate voice.”
What about that other famous Tory green, Boris Johnson? Deadpan, Miliband replies: “Johnson will not be an envoy, I can exclusively tell you.”
It was Miliband who, as party leader, persuaded Starmer to stand in 2015 in the safe seat of Holborn and St Pancras, which had been vacated by Frank Dobson. “[Keir and I] met through a mutual friend in 2008 and I immediately saw somebody of great decency and integrity,” he says.
Miliband is also close to Rachel Reeves: she backed him for the leadership in 2010 and served in his shadow cabinet. When they returned to the back benches in the Jeremy Corbyn years they had neighbouring offices in Portcullis House. And it was in fact Reeves, rather than Miliband, who in September 2021 first announced the figure of £28 billion for climate investment, saying she wanted to be “Britain’s first green chancellor”.
That was a different time. It was just before the Cop26 summit in Glasgow, when climate was at the top of the political agenda and Johnson, prime minister at the time, was happy to take part in a net zero arms race. Perhaps more important, interest rates were at a historic low. Behind Miliband’s back, critics whisper that Starmer keeps him in the cabinet because he owes him for his safe seat. There are also many within the party who have doubts over Miliband’s credentials and see his overt pursuit of the green agenda as a continuation of his perceived naivety. “Lots of people got burnt when he was leader,” one insider says, pointing out that many MPs lost their seats in 2015. “He also opened the door to Corbyn with his membership changes.”
And then there is the cost. Certain groups within the Labour Party fear that the £28 billion-a-year price tag has given the Tories an easy target ahead of the election. “Just Stop Oil is writing Starmer’s energy policy,” is one attack line that Sunak has already tested. Another is the claim that such spending could push up inflation and interest rates.
“Twenty-eight billion is a big-sounding number,” says Robert Ford, professor of political science at the University of Manchester. “It would look good on a poster and it will sound scary to people.” It also punches what Ford calls Labour’s “political bruise” — the idea that the party falls short when it comes to fiscal responsibility.
Since Reeves announced last year that the £28 billion would be phased in over the course of the parliament, rather than spent in full in year one, and would include the £8 billion to £10 billion the Tories already put towards green programmes, there has been speculation that the plan will be watered down further or ditched altogether. When Labour failed to win the Uxbridge by-election last year, which was widely blamed on the expansion of London’s ultra-low emission zone (Ulez), there was speculation that Miliband, the face of green Labour, might even lose his place in the shadow cabinet.
“The reshuffle after Uxbridge was a moment of jeopardy for Ed,” one Labour insider says. “But it is looking like he is stronger after that.” Starmer put the green prosperity plan at the heart of his party conference speech in September and this month said the argument over the scheme was “a fight I want to have”.
Nevertheless, it is likely the £28 billion figure will be cut back — and may not even make it into the party’s election manifesto. Reeves has said any funding will have to fit within her “fiscal rules” of reducing debt over the lifetime of a Starmer government. That decision, if it comes, will be made after Jeremy Hunt’s budget in March, when Reeves will reassess the economic outlook.
Even if it is slashed, insiders say the spirit of Miliband’s plan will survive, however. The manifesto will focus on GB Energy, localised power plans and “liberating the private sector” to free up capital.
One Labour frontbencher said: “The £28 billion is not set in stone. It might have to adapt to evolving circumstances. But the idea that the green agenda is going to be junked at some point I just don’t buy. It’s too central to the growth plan.”
And it is not just loyalty that has persuaded Starmer and Reeves to persist with the Miliband project. Polling suggests that many voters, particularly in the fabled Red Wall, are persuaded by the need to decarbonise the economy. Steve Akehurst, a pollster, said in a recent report that the energy security message — reducing reliance on foreign gas — was particularly effective at pinching votes from the Tories.
Supporters say it is this strategic thinking that shows Miliband is far from a naive idealist. “In no way is Ed a hairshirt activist,” one shadow minister says. “He is a politician at heart. He has a bold vision but is pragmatic about how you achieve these things. He knows we have to take people with us or we won’t get there.”
Miliband will have to use this political skill to sell Labour’s pledge to end oil and gas exploration in the North Sea — which has attracted fury from the GMB union. But Joss Garman, a former Labour staffer who during Miliband’s time in government was political director of Greenpeace, points out that he has shown this pragmatism before. In 2008 he was under intense pressure to stop a new wave of coal-fired power stations being built, but faced opposition within the cabinet and from unions. “He didn’t just ban them,” Garman says. “He said you can build them but only if you can reduce emissions. He called the industry’s bluff [the claim that it could economically capture and store its emissions]. He balanced the political considerations and worked out how far he could go without overreaching.” At that time coal provided 34 per cent of British electricity; now it provides 1.5 per cent.
“Ideas are the most underestimated commodity in British politics,” Miliband says. “Why is Rishi Sunak in such difficulty? Yes, he’s the fag end of five prime ministers. But his fundamental problem is he has no project for the country. He thinks that by working hard and reacting to events he can succeed. And he is wrong — if you have no project to change the country there is no point in being there.”
So where did his idealism come from? Miliband puts it partly down to his apprenticeship under Blair, who was obsessed with modernising the country, and, even more so, Brown, who was driven by a deep sense of public service. But it also comes from his family.
“Look, it wasn’t all Marx for breakfast and Hegel for lunch,” he says. But his parents, and their experience of surviving the Holocaust, instilled in him a sense that he had to improve the world. “To go through that experience, how can you not think that politics matters?” he says. “My grandfather was killed in a concentration camp. Both families were uprooted. It gave them a sensibility and seriousness. I don’t want to sound pious about it, but it gave them a sense of responsibility, a sense of responsibility to the world around you.”
He pauses. “That can be a burden as well as a blessing. Green Ed, Red Ed — other people can comment. But when people say, ‘You are an idealist,’ that I want to prevent this existential crisis for the world, well, yes, I’d say that’s a pretty important thing to care about.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.title: Greta Thunberg’s case thrown out over police conduct
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.subtitle: Judge rules that authorities attempted to impose ‘unlawful’ conditions during climate protest in October 2023
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.text:
A judge threw out charges against Greta Thunberg and four other activists after finding that police had attempted to impose “unlawful” conditions during an environmental protest.
The Swedish climate change activist, 21, was arrested for demonstrating outside the InterContinental London hotel on Park Lane on October 17, where heads of the world’s largest oil and gas companies were gathering for the annual Energy Intelligence Forum.
Thunberg, two Fossil Free London (FFL) protesters and two Greenpeace activists had pleaded not guilty to breaching Section 14 of the Public Order Act 1986, which allows the police to impose conditions on public assemblies deemed necessary to prevent serious disruption.
However, after a two-day hearing at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Friday, District Judge John Law found that the condition placed on the demonstration was “so unclear that it was unlawful” and that those who did not comply committed no offence.
Law also found there was insufficient evidence that the protest was causing serious disruption, as the entrance to the hotel had been cleared by the time of the arrests, rendering the condition “unnecessary”.
Protesters had blocked entrances to the InterContinental earlier that day, although the prosecution conceded that they had made a path on two occasions for people who were trying to leave the building.
“It is quite striking to me that there were no witness statements taken from anyone in the hotel, approximately 1,000 people, or from anyone trying to get in,” the district judge said.
“There was no evidence of any vehicles being impeded, no evidence of any interference with emergency services, or any risk to life.”
The condition imposed on protesters to move to a nearby location was “becoming increasingly garbled and confused as it was passed on from officer to officer”, he continued, adding that protesters had also not been given sufficient time to comply.
The officer who arrested Thunberg said he had told her to move to “Piccadilly Place”, a location that does not exist in London.
PC David Lawrence told the court: “I asked what her intentions were and asked if she wished to remain and she would be arrested, and if she wanted to leave and continue her protest on the pavement. She replied in words, by saying: ‘I’m staying.’”
Law said that the protest was “throughout peaceful, civilised and non-violent” and criticised evidence provided by the prosecution about the location of where the demonstrators should be moved to, saying the only helpful footage he received was “made by an abseiling protester”.
He added that “excellent soundproofing” had also “diminished the extent of intrusion”.
The judge said he would grant defence lawyer Raj Chada’s request for the government to pay his legal fees and Thunberg’s travel costs.
“We must remember who the real enemy is,” the Swedish activist said on Thursday outside court after the first day of trial. “What are we defending? Who are our laws meant to protect?”
Thunberg has been arrested several times over the last year during climate protests across Europe.
In October she was fined by a Swedish court for disobeying police at a demonstration at an oil terminal in Malmo, pledging afterwards to continue to protest even if it “leads to more sentences”.
Speaking after the hearing, Chada told reporters that the charges were “unlawful because they disproportionately interfered with our client’s right to free speech.”
“The government should stop prosecuting peaceful protesters and instead find ways to tackle the climate crisis,” he said.
Asked whether civil action would be taken against those who prosecuted the case, Chada said that “all options” would be explored.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/as-t.title: As the air goes out of Just Stop Oil, new tyre deflaters hit the streets
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/as-t.subtitle: Climate campaigners now accept they have to get the public onside more so than polarise them
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/as-t.text:
On Tuesday morning, Jess Knowles carried her 20-month-old son Rico out of her terraced Victorian home in southwest London in a mad rush, conscious that she probably could not waste a minute if she was to make it on time to her child’s hospital appointment.
The stay-at-home mum was greeted by a disastrous sight after she walked over to the driver’s side of her black Jeep Night Eagle, a sports utility vehicle (SUV) that she uses through her disabled father’s mobility allowance — two deflated tyres.
After initially fearing that the tyres had been slashed, Knowles, 36, found that the valve caps had been stuffed to make them deflate, one with sunflower seeds and the other with crushed shards of pasta — a simple yet effective foil that meant that she could not make her son’s appointment.
Knowles’s car was one of over 40 SUVs and sports cars on the narrow tree-lined streets of Sands End to be targeted on Monday night by the Tyre Extinguishers, a group of activists aiming to “make it impossible” for city dwellers to drive “polluting death machines”.
The group, which launched in 2021, is a decentralised movement, with instructions on how to deflate a tyre with something as small as a lentil available on their website along with leaflets to be placed on people’s cars to explain the action.
Activists under the banner of the Tyre Extinguishers, who have no affiliation with campaign groups such as Just Stop Oil or Extinction Rebellion, have been taking their war to SUVs all over the world, including countries as far afield as Romania, America and Australia.
CCTV obtained by The Times showed three men wearing baseball caps tinkering with tyre valves in Sands End on Monday night, with the whole operation lasting just under a minute for each car.
“It’s so bad. They said that they’d keep doing it unless you change your vehicle,” Knowles said. “I’m looking out the window at night just to see if they’re outside. I don’t want anyone near my vehicle. They could put the wrong thing in there, they could flatten it for all I know… They don’t know why people need a vehicle.”.
Knowles did not display her badge when she parks at home because she has a residency permit, leaving her a target in the eyes of the Tyre Extinguishers, who claim to not target mobility vehicles if they see a disabled badge.
The action comes as The Times has learnt that Just Stop Oil, which has not held a protest since early December, will be launching a new campaign to lobby Labour candidates to sign a pledge that they will resign if a Labour government signs new oil and gas contracts.
The move represents a significant step by the group to engage in electoral politics. The Times understands that it was in part prompted by a belief that JSO had effectively sounded the alarm around the impact of new oil and gas contracts and that the next step would be political engagement.
A source told The Times that it represents a “diversification of tactics” and that “there was still a place for cultural actions” such as protests at the National Gallery.
“It’s about people in their community and in their regions kind of trying to take the power back and exercise their own autonomy to political actors that don’t represent them,” a source said.
“Given it’s an election year, politicians have to emerge from their shells. They have to crawl out the cracks and holes under the floorboards so we’re going to take this opportunity to engage with them directly,” the source added.
This comes as Roger Hallam, the co-founder of XR, Insulate Britain and JSO, has called for the need for balance in the climate movement and for activists to begin preparing for societal collapse.
The change, which is motivated by his belief that climate change will no longer be stopped, is a significant departure from Hallam’s previous position on the importance of public disruption to enact change, an approach that made him the architect one of the most disruptive and radical protest movements in modern British history.
In his New Year address, he told his followers he was working on a “profoundly different framing” for 2024.
“It goes something like: ‘Look, the carbon regime has totally f***ed up so the climate crisis is now locked in. We don’t need to create massive social disruption because it’s going to happen anyway! The regime will collapse under the weight of its own contradictions. So, what next? We need to build the next civilisation and stop fascism from taking us to a terminal hell’. Bit long but you get the idea,” he said.
Hallam said that he would outline different aspects of a “balanced revolution” by working on ideas such as how to hold public assemblies, how to door-knock and how to stand in elections.
“The mission is to empower people to see the big picture — one that transcends the traditional categories of politics, economics, social connection, and spirituality in favour of a new fusion of confrontation and dialogue,” he said.
This also comes as the Reverend Mark Coleman, a climate campaigner who has twice been jailed for participating in Insulate Britain and JSO actions, stands for election in the upcoming Rochdale by-election.
Gail Bradbrook, another co-founder of XR, told The Times that the climate protest movement was incredibly focused on “preparing for the collapse of civilisation” by creating local assemblies to make decisions for the best of their community.
Bradbrook said that XR’s announcement last year that it would move away from disruptive tactics such as roadblocks and smashing windows was partly adopted because the tactic was being done by JSO.
“We [the climate protest movement] have to be more like nature,” she said. “Nature has ecosystems. It has different creatures for different purposes and they come alive at different times for different seasons.”
However, some experts believe that JSO has not been successful in holding protests of note in recent months and that this stagnation could give way to a newer more radical group to grow out of it.
Dr Paul Stott, of the Policy Exchange think tank, said that JSO has had little momentum in recent months due to its members being embroiled in legal battles, leaving the group needing to reinvent itself after running out of activists.
Last year during JSO’s last wave of action, the Metropolitan Police arrested 630 protesters from October 30 to December 4, with JSO data showing at least 276 people charged, more than 120 of whom under section 7 of the Public Order Act 2023, a new power that bans any action that “interferes with the use or operation of any key national infrastructure”. Some cases arising in 2023 are now being listed in the crown court in 2025.
On Monday, three trials are due to begin involving climate activists, including five XR protesters charged with criminal damage for breaking glass at JP Morgan’s European Headquarters in 2021, eight Insulate Britain campaigners charged with public nuisance for stopping traffic on the M25 in the same year, and five JSO activists charged with conspiracy to cause a public nuisance for occupying tunnels close to Grays Oil Terminal in 2022.
This comes before the Court of Appeal considering whether the protesters can argue as a defence their belief that the property owner would have consented to the damage caused if they had been fully aware of the impact of climate change. The case has been prompted by the attorney-general, Victoria Prentis KC, after a spate of acquittals of protesters who have defaced buildings.
“One of the problems they’ve had is they’ve had so many court cases and people being arrested, re-arrested and convicted. Once organisations get into that position it becomes tricky,” Stott said. “They’ve been tied up in prison support campaigns and that sort of prison support although it’s necessary to maintain the morale of the group and its prisoners and their families, it rather saps the energy out of the campaigns”.
“One thing Roger Hallam tends to do is start campaigns and those campaigns have a high profile,” he said. “Insulate Britain for example hadn’t achieved its aims but the campaign petered out and was replaced by Just Stop Oil. It is more likely that another organisation will be started this summer, will flare, have some success, and fade again”.
However, some in the wider climate movement believe that there is growing awareness that a polarising approach will not bear fruit in trying to prevent climate change and prepare for the impact it will have on the world.
Rupert Read, a former member of XR and a founder of the Climate Majority Project, said that the group, which aims to bring the public along with it has welcomed a significant number of people with backgrounds in XR, Insulate Britain and JSO on to its email lists.
“The climate movement is moving in the direction of understanding that engagement needs to be much wider and that the majority of people ultimately need to be onside for this to work. You can’t win by [being] endlessly polarising,” he told The Times.
“There’s always going to be space for civil disobedience and the situation that we’re in merits all kinds of approaches to be tried. But it is absolutely imperative that we get more and more people onside, that we depolarize, that we ensure that climate is not a culture war issue.”
“What we’re trying to do fits in with the change in XR strategy last year to a somewhat more moderate direction… there is a lot of people a lot of thoughtful people from XR who understand what’s going on and can smell the coffee… ultimately, you have to do something more than raise the alarm.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/chri.title: Chris Packham: My support for Just Stop Oil is conditional
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/chri.subtitle: Presenter and environmental activist was giving evidence as a defence witness in the trial of a protester
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/chri.text:
Chris Packham has told a court that he “selectively” supports Just Stop Oil but does not back all that they do.
The broadcaster and environmentalist, 62, made the comments while giving evidence as a defence witness in the trial of Cressida Gethin.
Gethin, a University of Cambridge music student, scaled a gantry above the M25, near Heathrow, during a Just Stop Oil protest in July 2022.
Cross-examined by Neil Griffin, for the prosecution, Packham said that his support for the environmental activist group was conditional.
Giving evidence at Isleworth crown court, west London, Packham said: “I selectively support things that they do. What they make of my support is up to them.
“I probably don’t support them in the way that they want.”
Packham, known for presenting BBC’s Springwatch and Winterwatch, was among those who became caught up in the disruption on the M25 — one day after the UK’s hottest temperature, of more than 40C, had been recorded.
Packham said that he came to “sympathise” with the fact that he was forced to think about climate change while being stuck for four to five hours during a trip from Hampshire to Surrey, where he was working on the BBC’s Inside Our Autistic Minds programme.
Gethin, who represented herself, asked Packham: “What were you feeling [when you were stuck]?”
Packham replied: “Initially I felt very frustrated and then obviously I researched, on trying to navigate a quicker route, I discovered the reason was that protesters were active on the M25, and then I changed my thinking.
“[I thought] I might as well use this to reflect again on why I am being delayed. That is what I chose to do. I sat and contemplated the reason that might have motivated the protesters to take that action.
“I thought about whether that action was productive and what it was doing. I took it as an opportunity to reflect on the fact I was in a traffic system sufficiently fragile, even normal disturbance would cause significant delay.
“I reflected on the fact that I was sweating quite profusely, it was a day after the UK had recorded its highest-ever temperature and two days previously the government’s net-zero plan had been declared illegal.
“I understood, I think, why protesters were taking their action.
“This led me to sympathise with the fact that I needed to be put in a position where I was forced to think about the gravity of the situation.”
Earlier on Wednesday, Gethin, who has taken two years out of her studies, insisted that she had faced a “massive moral dilemma” by engaging in the protest.
She denies one count of causing a public nuisance contrary to the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022. She does not dispute scaling the gantry but denies that it amounts to the charge.
The trial continues.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.title: Greta Thunberg laughs in the dock as oil protest trial begins
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.subtitle: The Swedish climate activist, 21, is accused of a public order offence during a meeting of oil executives at a hotel in Mayfair
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/gret.text:
Greta Thunberg laughed and wiped her eyes in court on Thursday as she went on trial accused of disrupting business leaders trying to develop “sustainable solutions to the world’s energy challenges”.
The Swedish climate activist, 21, is charged with a public order offence after being arrested while protesting outside a gathering of fossil fuel executives in central London last year.
Thunberg, two Fossil Free London (FFL) protesters and two Greenpeace activists appeared at Westminster magistrates’ court for the start of a two-day trial after each pleaded not guilty in November to breaching Section 14 of the Public Order Act 1986. If found guilty they face fines of up to £2,500.
Thunberg, flanked by environmental protesters and wearing a grey T-shirt with the motto “Hide a refugee and if that becomes illegal hide too” in Swedish, found it hard to keep a straight face during the prosecution’s opening remarks.
The court heard how she had been given a “final warning” by police to move to a designated protest area before being arrested outside the InterContinental Hotel in Mayfair on October 17.
Luke Staton, prosecuting, said leaders from the energy, finance and business worlds were present at the Energy Intelligence Forum, whose “stated aim” was to develop “sustainable solutions to the world’s energy challenges”, prompting laughter from Thunberg and the other defendants. Critics have dubbed the event the “oily money conference”, a nod to its previous name, the Oil & Money Conference.
The court heard that protesters started to gather at around 7.30am and police engaged with them about improving access for about 1,000 people inside the hotel, which had been made “impossible”.
Staton said some protesters gained access to the roof just before 10.30am and “were slowly abseiling down the side of the building”.
Superintendent Matthew Cox, the most senior officer on the scene, said police were able to negotiate with the protesters to allow a group of 30 delegates with flights to catch to leave the hotel. A “small family group” were also permitted to leave but struggled to get their buggy through the demonstrators who had allowed them only a narrow gap, he added.
He told the court that a group of around ten drummers were generating “quite a deafening noise” and that other protesters were letting off smoke flares.
At 12.30pm he decided to impose a section 14 condition, which dictated that the protest could continue but on the pavement to the south of the hotel. He told the court it was necessary “to minimise disruption to the protest while allowing the hotel and its guests to continue in some form of normality”.
The court heard that from 1pm officers engaged with individual protesters and informed them of the section 14 condition and of the designated protest area.
Thunberg was standing outside the hotel entrance when an officer told her that failing to comply with the condition would result in her arrest, the prosecutor said.
While that officer was engaged elsewhere, another officer then spoke with Thunberg and “gave her a final warning”.
“She said that she was staying where she was and so she was arrested,” Staton said.
The other defendants were similarly informed of the section 14 condition and did not move to the designated protest area, the court heard.
The arrests were made after Suella Braverman, then the home secretary, used a statutory instrument to lower the threshold for what kind of activity is considered “serious disruption”.
Staton said: “The Crown’s case is that all five of these defendants took part in a public assembly.
“They knew or ought to have known that a section 14 condition had been imposed and they all failed to comply with that condition.”
Thunberg arrived at the court just after 9am and made her way past media and environmental protesters who were demonstrating “in solidarity” with the defendants, holding up large yellow banners that read “Climate protest is not a crime” and cardboard signs saying “Who are the real criminals?”.
The trial continues.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/with.title: ‘With my stalker released, I watch where I walk’: MPs share safety fears
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/with.subtitle: Amid the Gaza vote acrimony, politicians speak out on trying to beef up office security and avoiding standing too close to the Tube platform edge
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/with.text:
MPs from across the political spectrum have told how they face death threats, intimidation and abuse in an attempt to “pervert our democracy”.
They spoke out after concerns were raised about the reaction to votes on a ceasefire in Gaza on Wednesday.
With tensions already running high on the emotive issue, acrimony broke out when Sir Lindsay Hoyle, the Speaker of the Commons, decided to break with parliamentary precedent to give Labour MPs an extra vote on their Gaza stance. This was against the advice of officials, but he said he was only trying to protect them from a possibly violent public backlash.
Penny Mordaunt, the leader of the Commons, accused Hoyle instead of having “raised temperatures”.
As the dust settled on the previous night’s mayhem, MPs gathered on Thursday to share stories about the intimidation and abuse they and their families had received in recent months.
“In order to be here at this time, I have delayed giving a personal statement to the police on the latest individual who thinks that members of this House are fair game to be harassed, stalked and threatened,” said Vicky Ford, a Conservative MP and former minister.
She voiced concern that “our votes are often wilfully misinterpreted and used to drum up hatred against parliamentarians, and that perverts our democracy”.
Such subjects are normally taboo in Westminster. MPs are afraid of speaking openly about the threats they face — to avoid making themselves a bigger target or giving perpetrators the satisfaction of knowing how deeply it impacts them.
One Tory MP privately said requests he made three years ago for security improvements in his office and another attempt to create a safe room in his home had come to nothing.
A minister also admitted they had decided not to stand at the next general election, not because they could not handle the threats but because it had become too much for their husband.
Lucy Powell, the shadow leader of the Commons, said many MPs did not want to be accused of complaining, but some felt they could stay silent no longer. “During recess we saw another line being crossed, with the intimidation of a member [of parliament] and their family at their family home,” she said.
Powell was referring to up to 80 pro-Palestinian protesters holding a demonstration outside the home of Tory MP Tobias Ellwood last week.
“Reports that other organisations will be targeting the homes of MPs ahead of and during the election have caused huge anxiety,” Powell said, in a reference to protest plans by Just Stop Oil. “It is a totally unacceptable development.”
Paul Bristow lost his job as a parliamentary private secretary back in November when he became one of the few Tory MPs to back a ceasefire. “Someone suggested on social media that they would show my wife a real man. Someone else suggested that they would attack me and my family,” he told the Commons this week.
Barry Shearman, a Labour MP for 45 years, also revealed he had received a death threat. “A gentleman was arrested and went into a mental institution,” he said. “When he was released, the House authorities and the Met police met me and said, ‘This gentleman is now out and he knows where you live’ … but that was the last I heard.
“I am a person who watches where he walks and does not stand by the side of the platform on the Tube. I alter my way of coming into the House. It is very stressful.”
Barry Gardiner, another Labour backbencher, complained recently that the security offered to MPs is “lamentably poor”. In a victim impact statement read out in court at the trial of a dentist who threatened to kill him, Gardiner said he was “aware members of parliament are increasingly being threatened and two of my colleagues have been murdered in the course of their work”.
However, he vowed not to let threats “reduce my accessibility to my constituents”.
Hoyle sought to stress this week how important the issue of MPs’ safety was to him. He made an emotional speech to parliament on Thursday saying he had given Labour a vote on its own Gaza ceasefire amendment because he felt a “duty of care” to MPs. “I never, ever want to go through a situation where I pick up a phone to find a friend, on whatever side, has been murdered by a terrorist,” said the Speaker. “I also do not want another attack on this House.”
UK Parliament said Commons officials worked closely with police forces, adding: “We cannot comment on MPs’ security arrangements or advice because we would not wish to compromise the safety of MPs, parliamentary staff or members of the public, but these are kept under continuous review.”
Lord Walney is the government’s independent adviser on political violence and disruption
The intimidation of MPs over their position on the Israel-Hamas conflict must stop. What is happening goes way beyond reasoned, impassioned debate and the right of citizens to petition their elected representatives.
Angry crowds surrounded the Palace of Westminster before this week’s votes, some chanting “intifada” and projecting an anti-Israel slogan onto the building itself.
MPs and their families are being targeted at home. Others have had their offices surrounded, occupied or vandalised. Streams of hateful correspondence are overwhelming parliamentary inboxes.
The spectacle of the Speaker of the House of Commons agreeing to change the usual procedures around votes to reduce the risk of violent reprisals against MPs must be the moment we wake up to this growing threat.
The prospect of violence is not theoretical speculation. Two MPs have been murdered in recent years, Jo Cox (obituary) by a far-right extremist and Sir David Amess (obituary) by a violent Islamist. Last year, the government rated the likelihood of an assassination of a public figure as above 25 per cent, the highest score in its updated National Risk Register — meaning that it is among the most likely risks facing the country.
Aside from the danger to individuals, the chilling effect on our political system is obvious. The pool of people prepared to serve our democracy in elected politics, which is already too small and unrepresentative, will shrink further if they believe putting themselves forward will bring an inevitable physical risk to them and their loved ones, or simply endless angry vitriol. And the foundation of that democracy will be undermined if extremists believe they can coerce MPs into doing their bidding by menacing them.
There are a number of steps we must take to ensure this week’s debacle in parliament marks a turning point.
The police must be consistent in their enforcement of existing powers to stop MPs being besieged in their homes. Deterring this unacceptable behaviour should surely take precedence over officers’ fear of inflaming situations simply by enforcing the law.
The government should urgently consider new measures to protect the space around sites that are vital to the functioning of democracy, such as MPs’ offices, council chambers and parliament itself.
Law enforcement agencies and public bodies must not shy away from publicly identifying and confronting the unholy alliance of far-left groups and Islamist extremists who are driving much of this intimidation.
And all mainstream political parties should commit to never again allow parliament to be cowed by a mob outside its walls, or by fear of reprisals waiting for MPs in their constituencies.
That means the scales must fall from the eyes of those politicians of the centre or left who for too long have wrongly believed that proposals to tackle extreme protesters and the ideologies that drive them were the real threat to our liberal democracy, rather than being necessary and welcome steps to protect it.

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/wild.title: Chris Packham: Birdsong gives us respite, solace and comfort
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/wild.text:
It’s late afternoon and Chris Packham is distracted by a blue tit on the bird feeder at his home in the New Forest. “And look, there’s a goldfinch and a greenfinch,” he says excitedly. Minutes later he spots a great spotted woodpecker and grins, then scowls as a grey squirrel chases it away. “I had a national rarity, a lesser spotted woodpecker yesterday — it woke me up drumming,” he says, taking a huge bite of vegan lemon polenta cake. “As a kid they were sufficiently common that I would find nests doing my paper round. They were part of our fauna even in suburbia. Now they have declined so far that having one here is a huge treat.”
Birds are Packham’s obsession, “not hobby”. The TV presenter, naturalist and activist can’t stop himself, but he knows birders can be intimidating. “People think you need expensive equipment but any cheap binoculars and bird feeder will do,” he explains. Now he has written Chris Packham’s Birdwatching Guide to encourage everyone, with easy instructions from how to use binoculars, which I have never understood, to identifying birds in flight.
The 62-year-old presenter wasn’t always into birds. “I was massively into animals from the moment I could crawl, particularly things I could pick up and touch and put into jam jars and study in my bedroom. But I didn’t encounter my first bird until I was five.” It was a dead starling he found in the gutter at a bus stop. “I was immediately entranced — it wasn’t squished, its feathers were beautiful, the colours fabulous, and I lit up at the sheer beauty and the intricacy of its wings. We were going to the stores and my mother told me to ‘put that revolting thing down’. I pretended to dump it but put it in my pocket and took it to my bedroom and examined it at night. I loved that starling. I opened its beak, I tried to open its eyes, I could feel its claws on my hand.”
But it wasn’t until Packham was 12 and his father bought him some cheap binoculars that he became addicted. “Under the tutelage of my excellent biology teacher, whom I saw yesterday, I started phasing out keeping animals in my bedroom and began watching them in the fields instead. I used to go after school to see a family of foxes and I began to notice the birds around me.”
His father bought him a field guide to British and European birds. Packham is still thrilled thinking about it. “He came home one Saturday with it and I set off immediately and cycled to the local river. I saw a bird that was yellow, scanned through the book, found the Baltimore oriole, an American species, cycled furiously home, ran up the driveway, burst into the lounge where my dad was watching the telly and told him. In his typically sober fashion my father took the book, nodded sagely and pointed out, as kindly as possible, that I had seen a grey wagtail. But I was a bird fanatic by then.”
He would set the alarm clock for excursions with his dad. “My father loved acquiring knowledge. He was massively into military history so you can test me on battle dates, but he got into natural history for me. I was very fortunate that first my parents allowed me to turn the house into a shit-covered menagerie of animals, then to roam around the countryside on my own. They were of the view that you went to school to learn the basics and you came back to be educated, so we spent every weekend at castles, art galleries, museums or looking at nature.” Even when his mother took him to see Shakespeare performed outside at the local abbey, he spent his time watching a kestrel’s nest. “I can still tell you a lot more about kestrels than Macbeth.”
• Birdwatching for beginners — Chris Packham’s guide
The British are fascinated by birds, which is strange because we have fewer species than on the Continent. “Did you know, in the UK in 2019 we spent £350 million on bird food, [while] the rest of Europe combined spent £150 million? It’s part of our culture. The only nations that seem to share our love are the Swedes, though the Dutch are quite big birders, and a few Germans. In Britain the RSPB charity has more than a million members — the French organisation has only 60,000.”
Packham doesn’t know why we are so intrigued by feathers. “Obviously we had that Victorian collecting bug when people collected bird eggs, but that can’t explain it all. Maybe we like being amateur naturalists. Or maybe it’s because we are an island with a limited amount of fauna. We only have 50-odd species of butterfly, a limited number of dragonflies, 18-21 bat species, but we still have 130 different breeding birds and 300 visiting. That’s where the diversity is.”
So is he a birder or more of a twitcher, determined to see how many species he can spot? “I tried twitching at university. I found it dissatisfying,” says the presenter, who is autistic, with customary bluntness. “For me just rushing round the country to see some rare little brown job in the bushes with a group of white blokes in waxed jackets in the rain didn’t tick my box. I was interested in the context of the bird — was it a beautiful encounter, was the light right, did I get a great view, how did it behave?”
• Chris Packham: Is It Time to Break the Law? review
Instead Packham prefers to settle down in a hide. “I saw the eyelashes of a black-tailed godwit the other day.” Birding is very therapeutic, he explains. “We know that people who have had significant surgery in hospital recover more quickly if they listen to birdsong. It’s deep-rooted and attaches us to nature, giving us respite, solace and comfort. All I got from twitching was tension, the anxiety of getting there, the ghastly one-upmanship. You’d drive miles home and it felt fruitless and disappointing.”
Other times Packham goes for walks and just listens. “I sometimes use the Merlin app [it can identify birdsong and calls] to remind me what I am hearing. It’s like learning a language, you can get rusty.” I still love a simple wood pigeon, I tell him — it reminds me of my childhood with my grandmother. “I love that monotonous cooing too. The repetitive nature means it’s not surprising. Song thrush and nightingales are more about the silences between the notes, which generate anticipation. It’s very exciting, like a Ramones gig, whereas the wood pigeon is more techno.”
During lockdown Packham spent hours listening to the orchestra of birds in the woods. “I was listening to firecrest and goldcrest, and I could hear them perfectly but I can’t any more. It’s age-related — I can’t hear bats any more either. It feels sad, so stop and listen while you can.” But he still has other subliminal encounters. “The piping call of the kingfisher and the flash I love, but the sparrowhawk is my favourite bird.” We have an affinity for owls in Britain, I suggest. “That’s quite recent — in the past they were seen as harbingers of bad luck, but crows are wiser and ravens the cleverest.”
Packham recoils from birds in cages but accepts captive breeding programmes. “We have lost 90 million birds in the past 50 years. That’s a shocker, an apocalypse. Meanwhile we have introduced 160 million pheasants each year to shoot them down. Think of the ecological damage: half of our UK biomass of birds is non-native pheasants and partridges, it’s bonkers.” He has tried to analyse why the British like to shoot. “It’s the whole psychosexual thing, the male thing, and the social side. It’s not necessarily a class thing, but it’s something for men to do, like going to the football.”
His greatest concern is the lead shot used on the majority of shoots, which he believes poisons the native birds too. “I would ban lead shot. Every winter my colleagues and I buy game in supermarkets and test them for lead, and last year we found one pheasant that was 3,200 times over the legal limit. I would also ban driven grouse shooting, it destroys moors. I am very glad that Labour have said they will ban fox hunting, but I will be keen to hold them to that. Having gangs of brutal savages killing wildlife for fun sends the wrong message to the young.”
• Chris Packham on Just Stop Oil and why he feels he’s let young people down
Farm management practices and pesticides have been another problem for birds, he says. “Intensive industrial agriculture has been a big driver — we need farmers to help encourage back species.” Pets are also an issue. “Everyone hits on cats and they do an enormous amount of damage, but dogs off the lead cause a huge amount of disturbance, particularly on nature reserves.”
Packham wants more urban nature reserves and wetland centres to encourage back species but also allow humans to observe them. “Ideally hides would have a coffee machine and a comfy chair. We have got to make sure that all communities can have access from a young age and we need new role models: top-quality Asian, black, trans birders. There have been too many Bill Oddies, David Attenboroughs and Chris Packhams — all white males.”
He also wants schools to encourage children to become birders as an introduction to nature. “When I was little I could roam where I wanted. Now we have imprisoned young people inside and the outside is seen as dangerous and dirty. But there isn’t a school playground that doesn’t have birds. Even in cities you might see jackdaws or a kite. It’s very soothing for children to observe. It’s certainly important for my mental health. The best things in life are birds and they’re free: no ticket required, no queue, no qualifications, little kit, just curiosity.”
Birdwatching Guide: from Beginner to Birder by Chris Packham (DK Publishing, £12.99)

image.caption: Chris Packham: “Nightingale song is very exciting, like a Ramones gig. Wood pigeon is more techno”KATIE WILSON FOR THE TIMES

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/stop.title: Stop eco warriors protesting at our homes, ministers urge police
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/stop.subtitle: A Just Stop Oil activist said the climate group was planning to directly target Labour politicians
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/stop.text:
Government ministers have called on the police to take an “extremely robust” approach against Just Stop Oil activists who are planning to occupy MPs’ homes before the general election.
The environmental campaigners notorious for blocking roads, defacing artworks and interrupting theatre shows and snooker championships are preparing to target elected politicians. Their tactics have been tested already, with protests before Christmas outside the homes of Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer.
A Just Stop Oil source said that visiting MPs at home was “not off the cards by any means” but reaffirmed the group’s commitment to non-violence.
“Our homes will be visited by floodwaters if politicians won’t end our dangerous and expensive addiction to oil, so it’s only fair that we pop by to remind them of this,” the source said. “It’s about people in their community and in their regions kind of trying to take the power back and exercise their own autonomy to political actors that don’t represent them.”
A minister said the police must protect politicians’ homes from campaigners. “These unhinged zealots are unable to win rational arguments and are unable to win elections so instead they resort to intimidation and harassment,” they said. “We cannot allow democratically-elected representatives of any party to be targeted by these mindless thugs, and we expect the police to be extremely robust in dealing with it.”
On Friday The Times revealed that Just Stop Oil would be targeting Labour MPs and candidates and encouraging them to sign a pledge to resign if a ­Labour government agreed any new oil and gas licences.
A subsequent investigation by The Mail on Sunday revealed that the group aims to target MPs’ offices and occupy them. “What our strategy is, at least in the short term, is that we’re going to be occupying Labour MPs’ offices, their houses, disrupting their speeches etc,” an activist told an undercover reporter. “The target is Labour MPs” although they “might just be targeting Tories too”.
Another activist said: “What this is going to mean is probably … bothering politicians, interrupting speeches, interrupting party conferences and being a bit shouty.”
Just Stop Oil confronted Labour last week by delivering letters to the offices of MPs and candidates demanding they resign unless a Starmer government revoked oil and gas licences.
Two ministers have written to chief constables urging them to protect MPs’ homes following a heated demonstration by anti-Israel demonstrators outside the Dorset house of the Tory MP Tobias Ellwood last week.
The police let campaigners stage a rally while holding placards depicting the Bournemouth MP’s face beside bloody handprints and the slogan “Complicit in genocide”.
Ellwood wrote: “Fellow MPs agree, we are witnessing a growing trend where public servants increasingly face intimidation and threats. Look at a parliamentarian’s email inbox and there is now a constant barrage of hate messages, not least against female MPs.”
Greenpeace protesters occupied the roof of the prime minister’s home in Yorkshire while he was on holiday last summer.
Mike Freer, Conservative MP for Finchley and Golders Green and a supporter of Israel, is resigning because of serious threats to his safety including narrowly escaping being murdered by the man who went on to kill his fellow Tory MP Sir David Amess. Jonathan Gullis, Conservative MP for Stoke on Trent North, told GB News that he had “bulletproof clingfilm” on the windows of his home and panic alarms in his bedroom.
Tom Tugendhat, the security minister, and Chris Philp, the policing minister, told chief constables that elected representatives must “feel safe in their homes, free from fear and harassment”, according to The Sunday Telegraph.
“The government has … confirmed that, where the facts support it so the conditions are met, section 42 of the Criminal Justice and Police Act 2001 can be used by the police to direct protesters away from a residential dwelling, in order to prevent harassment alarm or distress to the resident.”
That law was introduced by Jack Straw when animal rights campaigners targeted directors of scientific research companies. It was used in December to protect Starmer from Just Stop Oil protesters who sang Christmas carols with a climate change twist outside his home.
Police have a legal armoury to protect MPs’ homes. Sections 4a and 5 of the Public Order Act 1986 criminalise causing harassment, alarm and distress through threatening and abusive behaviour.
Aggravated trespass is an existing offence, and police also have powers to impose conditions on marches and assemblies, including gathering outside someone’s house, under sections 12 and 14 of the Public Order Act 1986, which could include getting them to move. There is also the Protection from Harassment Act 1997.
A Just Stop Oil spokesman said in response to the minister’s claims: “What is becoming self-evident to the majority of people in this country is that the ‘unhinged zealots and mindless thugs’ you reference, are the people running this country.”

image.caption: Just Stop Oil is known for blocking roads but has also protested outside the homes of politiciansVUK VALCIC/ALAMY

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/camb.title: Cambridge student convicted of M25 protest for Just Stop Oil
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/camb.subtitle: Cressida Gethin, 22, who was backed by the BBC presenter Chris Packham during her trial for causing public nuisance, said she did not expect to cause such disruption
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/camb.text:
A Cambridge University student has been convicted of causing a nuisance after scaling a gantry over the M25 during a Just Stop Oil protest.
Cressida Gethin, 22, was said to have delayed almost 4,000 Heathrow passengers by taking part in the demonstration on July 20, 2022 — a day after the temperature reached 40C for the first time in the UK.
Isleworth crown court was told the music undergraduate, who has taken two years out of her studies, aimed to “interrupt business as usual” and draw attention to the “dire situation” represented by the record heatwave.
On Monday jurors convicted her by a 10-2 majority of causing a public nuisance contrary to the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022. Gethin, who represented herself, did not dispute scaling the gantry but argued that the consequences did not amount to the charge. She will be sentenced on May 3.
During her trial, the court was told that Gethin had refused to come down despite warnings by the police that she was causing disruption.
Neil Griffin, for the prosecution, said: “What she did prevented thousands of people from being able to freely use the M25 and the surrounding roads. It’s not for one individual to say, ‘I believe in this so I’m going to stop you from using this motorway, I’m going to make your life miserable for hours and hours and hours’.”
Some 3,923 British Airways customers were affected by cancellations and delays, the court was told.
Chris Packham, the broadcaster and environmentalist, gave evidence as a defence witness. He said he came to “sympathise” with the protesters while stuck in traffic for more than four hours on the way from Hampshire to Surrey, where he was working on a BBC programme.
Packham, 62, told the court: “Initially I felt very frustrated and then obviously I researched, on trying to navigate a quicker route, I discovered the reason was that protesters were active on the M25, and then I changed my thinking. I sat and contemplated the reason that might have motivated the protesters to take that action.
“I reflected on the fact that I was sweating quite profusely, it was a day after the UK had recorded its highest-ever temperature and two days previously the government’s net zero plan had been declared illegal. This led me to sympathise with the fact that I needed to be put in a position where I was forced to think about the gravity of the situation.”
He also said he “selectively” supports Just Stop Oil but does not back all that they do.
Gethin broke down during cross-examination, telling the court she faced a “massive moral dilemma” by engaging in the protest.
She told the jury she did not expect it would shut all the lanes, and that she was unaware she was so close to Heathrow.
Asked if she intended to cause “spectacular disruption” she said she did not but soon “realised this was potentially a more effective protest than I thought it would be”.
Just Stop Oil, an offshoot of Extinction Rebellion, the global environmental campaign group, has conducted orange-themed protests to bring attention to the climate crisis. Actions have included throwing tomato soup over a Van Gogh painting at the National Gallery and scaling the Queen Elizabeth II Bridge over the River Thames between Kent and Essex.

image.caption: Cressida Gethin was supported by the BBC broadcaster Chris Packham during at her trial at Isleworth crown courtLEON NEAL/GETTY
